AI Factory Case Studies · Part 10 · The bets compared

Nine AI Factories, One Map: Which Bets Are Winning?

Over nine case studies we visited the largest AI factories on Earth, from a converted Memphis factory to a Norwegian fjord. Each made one big bet: speed, outside capital, a network of sites, its own chips, any building that holds a GPU, a decade-long head start, debt, brute force, or national strategy. This final part puts them side by side on one timeline and one scoreboard, and pulls out the patterns that matter more than any single site.

3. How big, really?

Part 1 showed three honest ways to count a gigawatt. Across the series, the headline figure was almost always the largest of them: a nameplate, a target or a campus plan. Estimates of power actually in use, mostly from Epoch AI, are smaller.

Headline vs estimated now

Megawatts, log scale. Grey is the headline figure; colour is the best estimate of capacity in use today (hatched where we found none and show the first tranche instead).

Google and China are left out: Google does not publish site sizes and runs a fleet, and China's capacity is spread across many state and company sites.

5. Five patterns

What the nine have in common

6. Who carries the risk

If AI revenue grows more slowly than AI spending, who pays? The series shows the answer is spreading. At Colossus, Fairwater, Rainier and Google, the owner carries most of it on its own balance sheet. At Abilene and Hyperion, investors and bondholders own most of the buildings. Neoclouds put it on lenders secured by GPUs. Utilities building gas plants for data centers put some of it, unless regulators prevent it, on ratepayers.

The risk chain

Tap a link. Arrows show who depends on whom being paid.

7. What to watch in 2027

Verdict: which bets are winning?No single bet is winning, and the strongest players are combining them. Speed wins the first year, as Colossus showed; outside capital wins the next gigawatt, as Abilene and Hyperion showed; own silicon and a long head start win on cost, as Google and Amazon are betting. The constraint underneath them all is power in the West and chips in China, and gas is filling the gap almost everywhere. The bet that will matter most over the next few years is the least visible: who carries the risk if demand disappoints, because that risk is quietly moving from the companies that use AI factories to the investors, lenders and ratepayers that fund them.

9. Reading the numbers

Sources
Every figure comes from Parts 1–9, which cite filings, company announcements, regulators, Epoch AI and the press, and flag secondary claims with ⚠️.
Timeline
Start points differ by site (land purchase, financing, announcement or construction start), so "days to first compute" compares like with like only roughly; each row states its start.
Sizes
"Now" values are Epoch AI estimates (Colossus 2, Abilene, Fairwater Atlanta, Rainier), CoreWeave's reported active power across 51 data centers, or the first tranche where nothing is running yet.
Scoreboard
Editorial 1–5 scores; higher always means better from that question's point of view (for example, a higher "neighbours" score means fewer local harms reported).
